items.subtype: Modifier placement: preposition + gerund opener (Despite originating from an insect ...), mid-sentence blank; the right subject is the insect’s song, a noun phrase built on the obvious noun
items.passage: The male lesser water boatman (Micronecta scholtzi) attracts mates through stridulation, rubbing a tiny ridged structure against its abdomen underwater. Despite originating from an insect only about two millimeters long, ______ reach roughly 99 decibels, rivaling the calls of far larger animals.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: the male boatman sings a courtship song that can
it is the male’s courtship song that can
researchers have found that the male’s courtship song can
items.explanation: The opening phrase, “Despite originating from an insect only about two millimeters long,” must describe the noun that comes right after it. What originates from the insect is its song, not the insect itself. Choice C places “the male’s courtship song” right after the phrase, so the sentence clearly says that the song originates from a tiny insect and still reaches roughly 99 decibels.

A.recipe: wrong noun as subject (W): the obvious noun, the insect
A.why_wrong: “The male boatman” follows the phrase, so the sentence illogically says that the boatman itself originates from an insect only about two millimeters long.

B.recipe: expletive opener (E): it-cleft with the right noun as its focus
B.why_wrong: The word that follows the phrase is “it,” so the phrase has no logical subject to describe; the song appears only after “it is.”

D.recipe: wrong noun as subject (W): a second participant, the researchers
D.why_wrong: “Researchers” follows the phrase, so the sentence illogically says that the researchers originate from an insect only about two millimeters long.

items.notes: Subject: lesser water boatman Micronecta scholtzi, a very loud song for its size (science). Real insect, facts kept general (males rub a small ridged structure against the abdomen; song measured at about 99 decibels in a 2011 study). No names. Band 7: the opener names the insect, so the obvious subject is the boatman, but what comes from the insect is its song (property key as in 2dd1b8bf, on the prep + gerund frame of 37e5c794). Recipes W, E, W. Key is the shortest option.
band7_moves: property key (band-7 file, section 3 move 7): the right subject is “the male’s courtship song,” a noun phrase built on the obvious noun, the boatman
the opener itself names the obvious noun (“an insect”), so A, which starts with that insect, reads naturally until the student asks what actually originates from the insect
B holds the right noun inside an it-cleft (E, as in 2bca654a); D starts with a second participant, researchers, then contains the key’s exact words
mid-sentence blank with 11 run words after it; all four options are grammatical and keep the same facts

band7.why: Property key built on the obvious noun (the male’s song, not the boatman), as 2dd1b8bf; the opener names “an insect,” so A, which starts with the boatman and keeps every fact, reads naturally (a garden path); B (it-cleft) and D (reporting frame) both contain the key’s words, as the foils of 37e5c794 all share its content. Caveat: the key is the shortest option, 5 words against 9.

items.subtype: Modifier placement: past participial comparison opener (Compared with those of humans), mid-sentence blank; plural “those” needs the plural property noun “the eyes of the helmet gecko”
items.passage: Compared with those of humans, ______ roughly 350 times more sensitive to color in dim light, allowing this nocturnal lizard to distinguish hues even by moonlight.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: the eyes of the helmet gecko are
the helmet gecko has eyes that are
the vision of the helmet gecko is
it is the helmet gecko whose eyes are
items.explanation: The opening phrase, “Compared with those of humans,” must be followed by the thing being compared, and “those” stands for that same thing. Only eyes can be compared with human eyes. Choice A places the plural noun phrase “the eyes of the helmet gecko” right after the phrase, so the sentence clearly compares the gecko’s eyes with those (the eyes) of humans.

B.recipe: wrong noun as subject (W): the obvious noun, the animal instead of its eyes
B.why_wrong: “The helmet gecko” follows the phrase, so the sentence illogically compares the gecko itself with the eyes of humans.

C.recipe: wrong head noun, sharing the key’s opening (the ... of the helmet gecko): singular “vision” cannot be what plural “those” stands for
C.why_wrong: The subject is the singular “the vision,” so “those of humans” has nothing to refer to; the sentence compares the gecko’s vision with an unnamed plural thing belonging to humans.

D.recipe: expletive opener (E): it-cleft with the right noun inside a relative clause
D.why_wrong: The word that follows the phrase is “it,” so the phrase has no logical subject to describe; the gecko’s eyes appear only inside the clause “whose eyes are.”

items.notes: Subject: nocturnal color vision of the helmet gecko (Tarentola chazaliae), shown by Swedish biologists in the 2000s (science). Facts kept to the well-known finding (the gecko sees color in dim light; its eyes were found to be about 350 times more sensitive to color than human eyes at that light level). No names. Band 7 on the comparison opener of 2dd1b8bf and fced396a, with plural “those” instead of “that” so that the deciding point is number as well as logic. One sentence, 26 words (models 13 to 41).
band7_moves: property key built on the obvious noun (section 3 move 7): “the eyes of the helmet gecko,” not “the helmet gecko”
comparison opener with plural “those,” so C, which shares the key’s shape (“the ... of the helmet gecko”) and keeps the same fact, fails only because its head noun is singular
B starts with the obvious noun (W); D holds the right noun inside an it-cleft (E)
four options of 7 or 8 words, all grammatical, same facts; key is not the longest

band7.why: Comparison opener with plural “those,” the 2dd1b8bf and fced396a pattern: B (the gecko has eyes) is the CB-style obvious-noun foil, and C (“the vision of the helmet gecko”) shares the key’s shape and fails only on number, so no option dies on one obvious fact.

items.subtype: Modifier placement: -ing participial opener (Sliding inward when pressed by the musician’s left hand), mid-sentence blank; the right subject is a part of the instrument (its keys), built on the obvious noun
items.passage: The nyckelharpa, a traditional bowed instrument from Sweden, takes its name from the rows of wooden keys mounted along its neck. Sliding inward when pressed by the musician’s left hand, ______ against a string, shortening its vibrating length and thereby raising the pitch.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: the nyckelharpa has keys that each push a small wooden blade, called a tangent,
it is the nyckelharpa’s keys that each push a small wooden blade, called a tangent,
the nyckelharpa’s neck holds keys that each push a small wooden blade, called a tangent,
the nyckelharpa’s keys each push a small wooden blade, called a tangent,
items.explanation: The opening phrase, “Sliding inward when pressed by the musician’s left hand,” must describe the noun that comes right after it. It is the keys, not the whole instrument or its neck, that slide inward when the musician’s left hand presses them. Choice D places “the nyckelharpa’s keys” right after the phrase, so the sentence clearly says that the keys slide inward and push the tangents against the strings.

A.recipe: wrong noun as subject (W): the obvious noun, the whole instrument
A.why_wrong: “The nyckelharpa” follows the phrase, so the sentence illogically says that the entire instrument slides inward when the musician’s left hand presses it.

B.recipe: expletive opener (E): it-cleft with the right noun as its focus
B.why_wrong: The word that follows the phrase is “it,” so the phrase has no logical subject to describe; the keys appear only after “it is.”

C.recipe: wrong noun as subject (W): another part of the instrument, sharing the key’s opening (the nyckelharpa’s ...)
C.why_wrong: “The nyckelharpa’s neck” follows the phrase, so the sentence illogically says that the neck of the instrument slides inward when the musician’s left hand presses it.

items.notes: Subject: the nyckelharpa, Swedish keyed fiddle, and its tangents (arts, music). Well-known facts (the name means roughly key fiddle; wooden keys pressed by the left hand push small wooden tangents against the strings to change the pitch). No names. Band 7 on the -ing frame of 2bca654a with the part key of 2dd1b8bf: the right subject is a noun phrase built on the obvious noun, and the strongest foil starts with that noun. Key is the shortest option. Review: C (the musician) replaced by the neck foil.
band7_moves: part key (section 3 move 7): the right subject is “the nyckelharpa’s keys,” built on the obvious noun, the instrument

A starts with the obvious noun (W) and keeps every fact; B holds the right noun in an it-cleft (E, as 2bca654a); C starts like the key (“the nyckelharpa’s”) but its head noun is the neck, the part the first sentence says the keys are mounted on
mid-sentence blank; all four options grammatical, 11 to 15 words, same facts

fixes: option C “a musician playing the nyckelharpa presses keys that ...” (ruled out on first read) replaced by “the nyckelharpa’s neck holds keys that ...”, which shares the key’s opening and fails only on its head noun; explanation, why_wrong and moves updated

band7.why: Even with the neck foil, the opener (“Sliding inward when pressed by the musician’s left hand”) fits only the keys, and only D makes the keys the subject; a foil whose head noun could plausibly slide (the tangents) would be a second defensible answer, so no fair lever to band 7 is left. Strong band 6, as the batch notes expected.

items.subtype: Modifier placement: noun-phrase appositive opener (One of the five great epics ...), mid-sentence blank; the work is the right subject, the heroine and her husband the wrong ones
items.passage: Tamil, a Dravidian language spoken primarily in southern India and Sri Lanka, possesses a literary tradition spanning more than two millennia. One of the five great epics of that tradition, ______ wrongly executed after being accused of stealing a queen’s anklet.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: Kannaki is the heroine of the Cilappatikaram, and her husband is
the Cilappatikaram tells the story of Kannaki, whose husband is
it is the Cilappatikaram that tells the story of Kannaki, whose husband is
Kannaki’s husband, whose story the Cilappatikaram tells, is
items.explanation: The opening phrase, “One of the five great epics of that tradition,” names a work of literature, so the noun that comes right after it must be that work. Choice B places “the Cilappatikaram” right after the phrase, so the sentence clearly says that the Cilappatikaram is one of the five great epics and tells the story of Kannaki.

A.recipe: wrong noun as subject (W): the heroine
A.why_wrong: “Kannaki” follows the phrase, so the sentence illogically says that a woman, Kannaki, is one of the five great epics of Tamil literature.

C.why_wrong: The word that follows the phrase is “it,” so the phrase has no logical noun to describe; the epic appears only after “it is.”

D.recipe: agent buried in a possessive (P): the possessive puts the husband first
D.why_wrong: The subject is “Kannaki’s husband,” so the sentence illogically says that her husband is one of the five great epics of Tamil literature.

items.notes: Subject: the Cilappatikaram (The Tale of an Anklet), Tamil epic (literature). Well-known facts (one of the five great epics of Tamil literature; Kannaki’s husband is wrongly executed for stealing the queen’s anklet). No author named. Band 6 by plan (R3_appositive has no band-7 official item): plain thing key after a noun-phrase opener, as 5b8f9cf2; recipes W, E, P. Key is not the longest option.

band7.why: R3_appositive has no band-7 official item, so it cannot be band 7; a strong band 6 on 5b8f9cf2 (the heroine and her husband as W and P foils).

items.subtype: Subject-verb agreement: singular head (method) behind a plural possessor (The Bechers’), with plural nouns and a relative clause with its own plural verb (were) between head and blank
items.passage: German photographers Bernd and Hilla Becher spent nearly five decades documenting industrial buildings. The Bechers’ method of photographing water towers and blast furnaces, many of which were soon to be demolished, from the same head-on angle under overcast skies ______ viewers to notice small differences among structures built for the same purpose.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The subject of the second sentence is the singular noun “method,” not the plural possessor “The Bechers’” or the plural nouns “water towers,” “blast furnaces,” and “skies” that come between the subject and the blank. The singular verb “invites” agrees with “method.”

A.recipe: wrong number, present (agrees with the plural possessor or the nearby plurals)
A.why_wrong: “Invite” is plural and does not agree with the singular subject “method.”

B.why_wrong: “Have invited” is plural and does not agree with the singular subject “method.”

C.why_wrong: “Are inviting” is plural and does not agree with the singular subject “method.”

items.notes: Subject: Bernd and Hilla Becher’s photographs of industrial structures (arts, photography). Real photographers; facts kept general (decades of head-on black-and-white photographs of water towers, blast furnaces and similar buildings, many later demolished, taken in flat overcast light). Band 7 on 863065c7: a possessor of the other number before the head (plural “Bechers’,” singular “method”) and a long intervener of plural nouns with its own plural verb (“many of which were”). Singular key; the other band-7 R1 item in this batch (w5b1_07) has a plural key.
band7_moves: possessor of the other number before the head (section 1): plural “The Bechers’” before singular “method”
intervener with its own finite verb of the other number (section 3 move 4): “many of which were soon to be demolished”
four plural nouns between head and blank (towers, furnaces, skies, plus the possessor); 26 words from head to blank; 13 run words after it

band7.why: As 863065c7: plural possessor before the singular head, four plural nouns and a relative clause with its own plural verb (“were”) between head and blank, 26 words apart; three plural foils in three tenses.

items.subtype: Finite vs nonfinite: to-infinitive of purpose after a compound predicate (stretched ... and then filled ...); three nonfinite or finite foils as in 3.19
items.passage: For several installations in the late 1990s, Brazilian artist Ernesto Neto stretched translucent, stocking-like fabric into elongated sacks and then filled them with powdered spices such as turmeric, cloves, and cumin ______ sculptures that visitors could experience through smell as well as sight.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The sentence already has its subject and both of its verbs: Neto “stretched” the fabric “and then filled” the sacks. The blank begins a phrase that explains why he did this. The to-infinitive “to create” correctly forms that phrase: he filled the sacks with spices in order to create sculptures that visitors could experience through smell.

B.why_wrong: Without a comma, “creating” attaches to the nouns right before it, so the sentence illogically suggests that the turmeric, cloves, and cumin were creating sculptures.

C.recipe: finite where a nonfinite is needed (third verb with no conjunction)
C.why_wrong: The finite verb “created” cannot follow “stretched ... and then filled” without a conjunction such as “and”; the sentence becomes a run-on list of verbs.

D.why_wrong: “And creating” is not parallel with the past tense verbs “stretched” and “filled,” and the participle “creating” cannot serve as a verb of the sentence on its own.

items.notes: Subject: Ernesto Neto’s spice-filled fabric sculptures of the late 1990s (arts). Real artist; facts kept general (sheer stretch fabric shaped into hanging sacks filled with spices such as turmeric, cloves and cumin). Band 6 by plan (R2_to_inf has no band-7 official item), on 3.19: purpose infinitive after a compound predicate, foils -ing without a comma (attaches to the nouns right before it), a third finite verb with no conjunction, and and + -ing.

band7.why: R2_to_inf has no band-7 official item, so it cannot be band 7; a close copy of the band-6 model 512f0ac9 (to forge / forging / forged / and forging).

items.subtype: Subject-verb agreement: plural head (anecdotes) behind singular nouns, a relative clause with its own singular verb (recounts) and an appositive with a second singular verb (presents); 19 run words after the blank
items.passage: Ihara Saikaku first won fame as a poet. The anecdotes of frugality and bankruptcy that Saikaku recounts in The Japanese Family Storehouse (1688), a book that presents itself as a practical guide to accumulating wealth, ______ a vivid portrait of Japan’s merchant class, whose prosperity was increasing even as its official social standing remained low.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The subject of the second sentence is the plural noun “anecdotes,” not “frugality and bankruptcy,” “Saikaku,” “The Japanese Family Storehouse,” or “a practical guide,” which all come between the subject and the blank. The plural verb “offer” agrees with “anecdotes.”

A.recipe: wrong number, present (agrees with “a book” or “a practical guide,” the singular nouns closest to the blank)
A.why_wrong: “Offers” is singular and does not agree with the plural subject “anecdotes.”

B.why_wrong: “Has offered” is singular and does not agree with the plural subject “anecdotes.”

D.why_wrong: “Is offering” is singular and does not agree with the plural subject “anecdotes.”

items.notes: Subject: Ihara Saikaku’s The Japanese Family Storehouse (1688), stories of merchants who make and lose fortunes (literature). Real writer and book; facts kept general (Saikaku first won fame as a haikai poet and turned to prose fiction in the 1680s; the book is framed as advice on getting rich; merchants ranked low in the official order though their wealth grew). Band 7 on 1c65db8f and ae439895: a plural head followed by a relative clause whose own subject and verb are singular (“Saikaku recounts”), then a singular appositive with its own singular verb (“a book that presents”).
band7_moves: intervener with its own finite verb of the other number (section 3 move 4): “that Saikaku recounts,” then “a book that presents itself”
plural head behind singular nouns (section 3 move 5): frugality, bankruptcy, Saikaku, The Japanese Family Storehouse, a book, a practical guide
25 words from head to blank, 19 run words after it, run of 46 words; plural key, singular foils in three tenses

band7.why: As 1c65db8f and b32eab9f: plural head behind six singular nouns, a relative clause with its own singular verb (“recounts”) and an appositive with a second singular verb (“presents”), 19 run words after the blank.

items.subtype: Subject-verb agreement: singular head (poem) with an appositive ending in a plural noun (stanzas) right before the blank
items.passage: Shota Rustaveli composed The Knight in the Panther’s Skin, widely considered the national epic of Georgia, around 1200. The poem, a celebration of friendship and chivalry narrated in roughly 1,600 four-line stanzas, ______ a central place in Georgian homes; for centuries, a copy was traditionally included in a bride’s dowry.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The subject of the second sentence is the singular noun “poem,” not the plural noun “stanzas,” which is part of the phrase that describes the poem. The singular verb “holds” agrees with “poem.”

A.why_wrong: “Hold” is plural and does not agree with the singular subject “poem.”

C.why_wrong: “Are holding” is plural and does not agree with the singular subject “poem.”

D.why_wrong: “Have held” is plural and does not agree with the singular subject “poem.”

items.notes: Subject: Shota Rustaveli’s The Knight in the Panther’s Skin, Georgian national epic (literature). Well-known facts (written around 1200, about 1,600 four-line stanzas, a copy traditionally part of a bride’s dowry). Medium on 2.20 and 2.21: one plural attractor inside an appositive just before the blank.

fixes: plainer words for register (“an important place in Georgian households” to “a central place in Georgian homes”; medium long-word share 15.3% to 13.9%, CB 12.5%)

items.subtype: Plural vs possessive nouns: two-slot grid (colony’s members), singular possessor cued by “a colony,” plain plural possessed noun
items.passage: Hutterites, members of a Christian community that immigrated to the northern Great Plains in the 1870s, live in agricultural colonies where all property is shared. When a colony grows to roughly 150 residents, its leaders purchase land for an additional settlement and divide the ______ into two groups, one of which will eventually relocate.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The blank names the people who belong to one colony. The passage refers to “a colony,” so the singular possessive “colony’s” is needed. “Members” is a plain plural noun that does not possess anything, so it takes no apostrophe.

A.why_wrong: “Colonies” is a plain plural, but the members belong to a single colony, so the singular possessive “colony’s” is needed.

B.recipe: needless apostrophe on a plain plural
B.why_wrong: “Colony’s” is correct, but “member’s” is a possessive form, and the members do not possess anything; the plain plural “members” is needed.

D.recipe: wrong possessor number and needless apostrophe
D.why_wrong: “Colonies’” is a plural possessive, but the passage refers to a single colony; “members’” adds a needless apostrophe to a plain plural.

items.notes: Subject: Hutterite colonies splitting in two at about 150 people (social science). Well-known facts (Anabaptist group that settled on the northern Plains in the 1870s, communal property, colonies divide when they grow large). Medium on 2.24: two-slot partial grid with a singular possessor cued in the same sentence.

items.subtype: Subject-verb agreement: compound subject (X and Y) followed by a singular “each” phrase
items.passage: Between about 100 BCE and 500 CE, Hopewell communities in present-day Ohio constructed massive earthworks in precise geometric shapes. The Great Circle and the Octagon at Newark, each enclosed by earthen walls hundreds of meters long, ______ among eight Hopewell sites inscribed on UNESCO’s World Heritage List in 2023.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The subject of the second sentence is the compound “The Great Circle and the Octagon at Newark,” which names two earthworks and is therefore plural. The phrase beginning with “each” describes the subject but does not make it singular. The plural verb “were” agrees with the compound subject.

B.recipe: wrong number, past (agrees with “each” or with one of the two nouns)
B.why_wrong: “Was” is singular and does not agree with the plural compound subject “The Great Circle and the Octagon at Newark.”

C.why_wrong: “Has been” is singular and does not agree with the plural compound subject.

D.why_wrong: “Is” is singular and does not agree with the plural compound subject.

items.notes: Subject: Hopewell Ceremonial Earthworks, Newark Great Circle and Octagon, UNESCO 2023 (history). Well-known facts (Hopewell earthworks in Ohio, about 100 BCE to 500 CE; eight sites inscribed in 2023). Medium on 2.13: compound subject with a trailing “each” phrase.

items.subtype: Modifier placement: preposition + gerund opener (After smoothing ...), mid-sentence blank; the women are the right subject
items.passage: In the Kassena village of Tiébélé in Burkina Faso, decorating house exteriors is traditionally women’s work. After smoothing a mixture of mud and dung onto a wall, ______ geometric designs in red, black, and white.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: the wall is decorated by the women with
the women’s next task is to paint
items.explanation: The opening phrase, “After smoothing a mixture of mud and dung onto a wall,” describes the people who do the smoothing: the women. Choice D places “the women” right after the phrase, so the sentence clearly says that the women smooth the mixture onto a wall and then paint geometric designs on it.

A.recipe: passive that leaves the wrong noun as subject (V)
A.why_wrong: “The wall” follows the phrase, so the sentence illogically says that the wall smooths a mixture of mud and dung onto a wall.

B.why_wrong: The subject is “the women’s next task,” so the sentence illogically says that a task smooths a mixture of mud and dung onto a wall.

C.why_wrong: The word that follows the phrase is “there,” so the phrase has no logical subject to describe.

items.notes: Subject: painted houses of Tiébélé, Kassena women’s wall designs, Burkina Faso (arts, architecture). Well-known facts (women decorate the houses; walls are plastered with mud and dung and painted in red, black and white). Medium on 2.17: short opener, plain agent key, recipes V, P, E. Key is the shortest option, as in 2.17.

items.subtype: Modifier placement: past participial opener (Patented in 1980), mid-sentence blank; the invention, named with a possessive, is the right subject
items.passage: During a career of more than three decades at NASA, data scientist Valerie Thomas managed computer systems that processed images transmitted by orbiting Landsat satellites. Patented in 1980, ______ to make a three-dimensional image appear to float in front of the viewer.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: Thomas invented the illusion transmitter; it uses two concave mirrors
Thomas’s illusion transmitter uses two concave mirrors
two concave mirrors are used in Thomas’s illusion transmitter
Thomas designed the illusion transmitter, which uses two concave mirrors
items.explanation: The opening phrase, “Patented in 1980,” describes something that received a patent: Thomas’s invention. Choice B places “Thomas’s illusion transmitter” right after the phrase, so the sentence clearly says that the illusion transmitter was patented in 1980 and uses two concave mirrors.

A.recipe: wrong noun as subject (W), person first, then a semicolon
A.why_wrong: “Thomas” follows the phrase, so the sentence illogically says that Thomas herself was patented in 1980.

C.recipe: passive that leaves the wrong noun as subject (V)
C.why_wrong: “Two concave mirrors” follows the phrase, so the sentence illogically says that the mirrors, rather than the invention that uses them, were patented in 1980.

D.recipe: wrong noun as subject (W), person first, then “which”
D.why_wrong: “Thomas” follows the phrase, so the sentence illogically says that Thomas herself was patented in 1980.

items.notes: Subject: Valerie Thomas, NASA, the illusion transmitter patented in 1980 (science, technology). Well-known facts (long NASA career on Landsat image processing; 1980 patent for a device that uses concave mirrors to create a floating three-dimensional image). Medium on 2.19: past participial opener about an achievement, possessive key, two person-first foils (semicolon and which, as in 2.19) and a passive foil.

items.subtype: Finite vs nonfinite: -ing participial phrase of result after a complete clause and comma
items.passage: Rüppell’s vultures, which inhabit the dry grasslands of the Sahel and East Africa, typically ride rising currents of warm air while scanning the ground for carcasses. In 1973, one of these birds collided with an airliner cruising roughly 11,300 meters above Côte d’Ivoire, ______ the record for the highest bird flight ever documented.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The second sentence already has a subject (“one of these birds”) and a main verb (“collided”). The blank begins a phrase that states the result of the collision. The participle “setting” correctly forms that phrase: by colliding with an airliner at that height, the vulture set a record.

A.recipe: finite where a nonfinite is needed (past)
A.why_wrong: The finite verb “set” would be a second main verb for “one of these birds” joined to “collided” with only a comma and no conjunction.

B.recipe: finite where a nonfinite is needed (present)
B.why_wrong: The finite verb “sets” would be a second main verb joined to “collided” with only a comma, and its present tense does not fit an event in 1973.

D.recipe: finite where a nonfinite is needed (past perfect)
D.why_wrong: The finite verb “had set” would be a second main verb joined to “collided” with only a comma and no conjunction.

items.notes: Subject: Rüppell’s vulture struck by an airliner at about 11,300 meters over Côte d’Ivoire in 1973 (science). Well-known record (highest documented bird flight). Medium on 2.9: complete clause, comma, result participle; foils three finite forms of the same verb.

review.notes: Not too close to live words_in_context.B1.easy.w2b3_12 (bar-headed geese): different bird, different premise (an altitude record set by an airliner strike vs flight paths that follow the terrain), different skill; no other Ruppell’s vulture item live or official.

items.subtype: Tense: simple present for a habitual action (Every year), present context
items.passage: For centuries, the Finnish city of Turku has marked the start of the Christmas holidays with a public ceremony. Every year at noon on December 24, a city official ______ the Declaration of Christmas Peace from the balcony of a building on the Old Great Square.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The phrase “Every year” shows that the sentence describes something that happens regularly, and the passage describes the tradition in the present (“has marked”). The simple present tense verb “delivers” fits this habitual action and agrees with the singular subject “a city official.”

A.recipe: past perfect where the cue is present
A.why_wrong: The past perfect “had delivered” describes an action completed before another past action, but the sentence describes a yearly ceremony that still takes place.

B.recipe: simple past where present is needed
B.why_wrong: The past tense “delivered” places the ceremony in the past, but “Every year” and the present context describe a ceremony that still takes place.

C.why_wrong: “Would have delivered” describes something that might have happened but did not, which does not fit a regular yearly ceremony.

items.notes: Subject (replaced in review): the Declaration of Christmas Peace in Turku, Finland, read from a balcony on the Old Great Square at noon on Christmas Eve (history, culture). Well-known facts, no person named. Easy on 1.17: explicit habitual cue in the same sentence, present perfect context; no present perfect foil.

fixes: subject replaced: the Nenets yearly herd migration cloned live form_structure_and_sense.R4_present.easy.w3b4_14 (Kyrgyz herders move livestock to summer pastures each spring, same template and tier) and sat beside official FSS reindeer items 59209b6d and 843f92af; new subject the Turku Declaration of Christmas Peace (grepped, claimed), same frame, options, recipes and key letter D

items.subtype: Pronoun-antecedent agreement: singular subject pronoun (it) for “its door”; foils plural personal pronoun and demonstratives
items.passage: Many historic buildings in Stone Town, the oldest district of Zanzibar City, feature massive wooden doors decorated with carved flowers, fish, and chains. Traditionally, a family commissioned its door before construction began, because ______ was intended to display the household’s wealth and status to everyone passing by.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The blank refers back to the family’s door (“its door”), which is singular. The singular pronoun “it” agrees with “door.”

B.why_wrong: “They” is plural and does not agree with the singular antecedent “door.”

C.why_wrong: “These” is plural and does not agree with the singular antecedent “door.”

D.why_wrong: “Those” is plural and does not agree with the singular antecedent “door.”

items.notes: Subject: carved wooden doors of Stone Town, Zanzibar (history, architecture). Well-known facts (doors carved with flowers, fish and chains; traditionally made before the house as a sign of status). Easy on 1.19 and 1.26: singular antecedent in the same sentence, all foils plural.

fixes: “before construction of the house began” to “before construction began”, so “it” has one candidate, the door

items.subtype: Pronoun-antecedent agreement: plural subject pronoun (they) for “hind wings”; foils singular personal pronoun and demonstratives
items.passage: Although most earwigs rarely fly, many species possess large, fan-shaped hind wings made of a delicate membrane. When not in use, ______ are folded into a compact packet a fraction of their unfolded size and protected beneath a pair of short, leathery forewings.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The blank refers back to the earwigs’ “hind wings,” a plural noun. The plural pronoun “they” agrees with “hind wings.”

A.why_wrong: “It” is singular and does not agree with the plural antecedent “hind wings.”

C.why_wrong: “This” is singular and does not agree with the plural antecedent “hind wings.”

D.why_wrong: “That” is singular and does not agree with the plural antecedent “hind wings.”

items.notes: Subject: earwig hind wings folded beneath short forewings (science). Well-known facts (earwigs rarely fly; large membranous hind wings fold into a small packet under short, hard forewings). Easy on 1.12: plural antecedent in the previous sentence, singular foils.

items.subtype: Subject-verb agreement: singular head (Nsibidi) behind a singular appositive
items.passage: Nsibidi, a centuries-old system of writing from the Cross River region of southeastern Nigeria, ______ used by the Ejagham and neighboring peoples to record messages, laws, and stories.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The subject of the sentence is “Nsibidi,” the name of one system of writing, so it is singular. The singular verb “was” agrees with “Nsibidi.”

A.why_wrong: “Are” is plural and does not agree with the singular subject “Nsibidi.”

B.why_wrong: “Were” is plural and does not agree with the singular subject “Nsibidi.”

D.why_wrong: “Have been” is plural and does not agree with the singular subject “Nsibidi.”

items.notes: Subject: Nsibidi, symbol system of the Cross River region (history, social science). Well-known facts (centuries old; used by the Ejagham and neighboring peoples). Easy on 1.4: singular head with a plain singular appositive, no number clash.

items.subtype: Subject-verb agreement: plural subject (these singers) right before the blank
items.passage: In Kurdish communities in eastern Turkey and northern Iraq, dengbêj are traditional storytellers who sing their narratives rather than speak them. Performing for hours at a time, these singers ______ tales of love, warfare, and exile entirely from memory, usually without any musical instrument.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The subject of the second sentence is the plural noun “singers.” The plural verb “recite” agrees with “singers.”

A.why_wrong: “Recites” is singular and does not agree with the plural subject “singers.”

B.why_wrong: “Is reciting” is singular and does not agree with the plural subject “singers.”

C.why_wrong: “Has recited” is singular and does not agree with the plural subject “singers.”

items.notes: Subject: dengbêj, Kurdish singers of long stories (social science, culture). Well-known facts (sung narratives performed from memory, usually unaccompanied). Easy on 1.34 and 1.6: plural subject right before the blank, no intervener.

items.subtype: Finite vs nonfinite: missing main verb after a subject with a participial phrase (Walls made of hempcrete)
items.passage: Hempcrete is a lightweight construction material made from lime, water, and the woody inner core of hemp stalks. Walls made of hempcrete ______ buildings effectively, keeping interiors warm in winter and cool in summer.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The second sentence has a subject (“Walls made of hempcrete”) but no main verb. The finite present tense verb “insulate” supplies it and agrees with the plural subject “Walls.”

B.recipe: nonfinite where a finite verb is needed (-ing)
B.why_wrong: The participle “insulating” cannot serve as the main verb of the sentence, which leaves the sentence without one.

C.recipe: nonfinite where a finite verb is needed (having + past participle)
C.why_wrong: “Having insulated” is nonfinite and cannot serve as the main verb of the sentence.

D.recipe: nonfinite where a finite verb is needed (to + base)
D.why_wrong: The infinitive “to insulate” cannot serve as the main verb of the sentence.

items.notes: Subject: hempcrete walls (science, engineering). Well-known facts (lime, water and hemp hurds; good insulation). Easy on 1.23 and 1.31: canonical set {finite, -ing, having + participle, to + base}.

items.subtype: Finite vs nonfinite: missing main verb after a subject with an appositive-like participial phrase (born around 1141 ...)
items.passage: Persian poet Nizami Ganjavi, born around 1141 in the city of Ganja in present-day Azerbaijan, ______ five lengthy narrative poems that were eventually assembled into a single collection known as the Khamsa (Quintet).
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The sentence has a subject (“Persian poet Nizami Ganjavi”) but no main verb; the phrase “born around 1141 ... Azerbaijan” only describes the poet. The finite past tense verb “wrote” supplies the main verb.

A.recipe: nonfinite where a finite verb is needed (-ing)
A.why_wrong: The participle “writing” cannot serve as the main verb of the sentence, which leaves the sentence without one.

C.recipe: nonfinite where a finite verb is needed (having + past participle)
C.why_wrong: “Having written” is nonfinite and cannot serve as the main verb of the sentence.

D.recipe: nonfinite where a finite verb is needed (to + base)
D.why_wrong: The infinitive “to write” cannot serve as the main verb of the sentence.

items.notes: Subject: Nizami Ganjavi and the Khamsa (literature). Well-known facts (born around 1141 in Ganja; five long narrative poems later collected as the Khamsa). Easy on 1.21: subject with a descriptive phrase, canonical finite set.

items.subtype: Plural vs possessive nouns: two-slot grid with an irregular plural (fly’s two eardrums), singular possessor cued by “The female ... fly,” “she” and “the fly”
items.passage: The female Ormia ochracea fly deposits its larvae on living crickets. To locate a host, she listens for a male cricket’s chirping song: although the ______ are separated by only about half a millimeter, they are mechanically connected, allowing the fly to determine precisely where a sound originates.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The blank names the eardrums of one fly (“The female Ormia ochracea fly,” “she,” “the fly”), so the singular possessive “fly’s” is needed. “Eardrums” is a plain plural noun that does not possess anything, so it takes no apostrophe.

A.recipe: missing apostrophe on the possessor and needless apostrophe on the plural
A.why_wrong: “Flies” is a plain plural, but the eardrums belong to one fly; “eardrum’s” adds a needless apostrophe to a plain plural.

B.recipe: needless apostrophe on a plain plural
B.why_wrong: “Fly’s” is correct, but “eardrum’s” is a possessive form, and the eardrums do not possess anything; the plain plural “eardrums” is needed.

C.why_wrong: “Flies’” is a plural possessive, but the passage describes the eardrums of a single fly.

items.notes: Subject: Ormia ochracea, a parasitoid fly that finds singing crickets with closely spaced, linked eardrums (science). Well-known facts (larvae deposited on crickets; eardrums about half a millimeter apart and mechanically coupled, giving precise direction finding). Easy on 1.36 and 1.16: full 2 x 2 grid with an irregular plural.

items.subtype: Finite vs nonfinite: to-infinitive of purpose after a complete clause
items.passage: Lac insects are tiny scale insects that feed on tree sap and gradually cover the branches with a protective resin. Farmers in India and Thailand cultivate the insects on host trees ______ this resin, which manufacturers refine into shellac for varnishes and coatings.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The second sentence is already complete: it has a subject (“Farmers in India and Thailand”) and a verb (“cultivate”). The blank begins a phrase that explains why the farmers cultivate the insects. The to-infinitive “to harvest” correctly forms that phrase.

A.recipe: finite where a nonfinite is needed (past)
A.why_wrong: The finite verb “harvested” would be a second main verb with no conjunction joining it to “cultivate,” and its past tense does not fit the present description.

C.recipe: finite where a nonfinite is needed (present)
C.why_wrong: The finite verb “harvests” would be a second main verb with no conjunction joining it to “cultivate.”

D.recipe: finite where a nonfinite is needed (present progressive)
D.why_wrong: The finite verb “are harvesting” would be a second main verb with no conjunction joining it to “cultivate.”

items.notes: Subject: lac insects raised on host trees for the resin refined into shellac (science, agriculture). Well-known facts (scale insects that secrete resin on branches; India and Thailand are major producers). Easy on 1.22 and 1.27: purpose infinitive after a complete clause, three finite foils.

items.subtype: Tense: past perfect for an action earlier than a past event (centuries earlier than 1963)
items.passage: In 1963, a resident of Derinkuyu, a town in central Turkey, demolished a wall while renovating his home and discovered a concealed passage. It led to an enormous underground city that inhabitants of the region ______ into soft volcanic rock centuries earlier.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The passage describes a discovery in 1963 and says the city was made “centuries earlier.” The past perfect “had carved” correctly shows that the carving happened before the 1963 discovery.

A.why_wrong: The future tense “will carve” places the carving after the present, but it happened centuries before 1963.

B.why_wrong: The present progressive “are carving” describes an action happening now, but the carving was finished centuries before 1963.

D.recipe: present simple where past perfect is needed
D.why_wrong: The present tense “carve” does not fit an action completed centuries before a past event.

items.notes: Subject: Derinkuyu underground city found in 1963 (history). Well-known facts (a resident renovating his house broke through a wall into a passage; the city is carved into soft volcanic rock and is centuries old). Easy on 1.24: “centuries earlier” than a dated past event; no simple past foil.

items.subtype: Finite vs nonfinite: second verb of a compound predicate (pursue ... and ______)
items.passage: Dholes are wild dogs that inhabit forests stretching from India to Southeast Asia. Hunting cooperatively in packs of up to thirty animals, dholes often pursue deer much larger than themselves and ______ to one another with distinctive whistles to remain together in dense undergrowth.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The blank follows “and,” so it must be the second verb of the predicate that begins with “pursue.” The finite present tense verb “call” is parallel with “pursue” and agrees with the plural subject “dholes.”

B.recipe: nonfinite where a finite verb is needed (-ing)
B.why_wrong: The participle “calling” is not parallel with the finite verb “pursue” and cannot serve as the second verb of the predicate.

C.recipe: nonfinite where a finite verb is needed (to + base)
C.why_wrong: The infinitive “to call” is not parallel with the finite verb “pursue” and cannot serve as the second verb of the predicate.

D.recipe: nonfinite where a finite verb is needed (having + past participle)
D.why_wrong: “Having called” is nonfinite and cannot serve as the second verb of the predicate.

items.notes: Subject: dholes, Asian wild dogs that whistle to keep the pack together (science). Well-known facts (packs of up to about thirty; prey such as sambar and chital deer; whistling calls in dense cover). Easy on 1.11: compound predicate, canonical nonfinite foils.
